To suborn someone means to secretly persuade, bribe, or pressure them into doing something illegal or morally wrong — something they wouldn't necessarily do on their own.

The key thing that makes this word special is the indirect structure of the wrongdoing. The person who suborns is not committing the bad act themselves. Instead, they are pulling strings behind the scenes — corrupting, inducing, or paying someone else to do the dirty work for them.

Think of it as: "I won't lie, steal, or break the law — but I'll get you to do it for me."

By far the most common place you'll encounter this word is in legal contexts, in the phrase "to suborn perjury."

Perjury means lying under oath in a court of law. To suborn perjury means to bribe or convince a witness (or anyone sworn to tell the truth) to lie on the stand. This is itself a serious crime — distinct from perjury itself — because you are the corrupt hand that made the lie happen.

Example:

The defense attorney was disbarred after it was discovered that he had suborned a witness — paying her $50,000 to claim she had seen his client somewhere else on the night of the crime.

Notice: the attorney didn't lie himself. He made someone else lie. That act of inducing the lie is the suborning.

While perjury is its most famous companion, suborn can apply to inducing any kind of wrongful or illegal act — not just lying in court. The common thread is always:

  • Someone is persuaded, bribed, or pressured into wrongdoing.
  • The person doing the suborning is working indirectly and often secretly.
  • The act being induced is illegal, corrupt, or a betrayal of duty.

More examples:

The mob boss suborned three city officials, paying them to look the other way while illegal construction proceeded.

The corporation's executives were accused of suborning accountants into falsifying financial records.

He suborned his own staff to destroy evidence before the inspection.

Understanding where a word ends is as important as understanding where it begins.

Suborn vs. Bribe: Bribery is about offering money or gifts to get a favor — legal or illegal. Suborning is more specific: it is always about inducing wrongdoing. Every act of suborning involves an element of bribery or corrupt inducement, but the emphasis is on the wrongful act being induced, not the payment itself.

Suborn vs. Persuade: Persuasion is neutral. You can persuade someone to eat healthier. You cannot suborn someone to eat healthier. Suborn carries the weight of moral corruption — it only applies when what you're inducing is wrong.

Suborn vs. Coerce: Coercion usually involves force, fear, or threats. Suborning leans more toward inducement — dangling a reward, not wielding a threat. That said, the lines can blur, and you can suborn someone through subtle pressure too.

Suborn vs. Abet: To abet is to assist or encourage someone who is already committing or planning a crime. To suborn is to be the very reason they commit the wrongful act — you are the originating force that sets the corruption in motion.
The Moral Weight of the Word

"Suborn" carries a sense of insidious, calculated corruption. The person who suborns is often shielded from direct guilt — they didn't steal, they didn't lie, they didn't forge. But they are morally (and legally) responsible for the wrongdoing because they engineered it from behind the curtain.

This is why the word appears so often in legal and political contexts — it describes a particular kind of villainy: the kind that keeps its hands technically clean while dirtying everyone around it.

It's worth noting: the person who is suborned — the one who takes the bribe and commits the act — is also guilty. Suborning doesn't excuse the person who does the actual wrong. Both parties bear responsibility. But the one who suborned is considered the deeper corruptor, the architect of the wrongdoing.
In a Sentence — Quick Reference Examples

• "She was charged with suborning perjury after two witnesses admitted she had paid them to lie."
  • "The general suborned his officers into covering up the massacre."
  • "An attempt to suborn the jury was discovered before the verdict was reached."
  • "He had been quietly suborning colleagues for months before anyone noticed the pattern of corruption."
To suborn is to secretly induce, bribe, or corrupt someone into committing a wrongful or illegal act — making you the hidden architect of someone else's wrongdoing.
